## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Gopakamoggallāna Sutta* (MN 108) is set at Rājagaha shortly after the passing away (*parinibbāna*) of the Buddha, against a backdrop of rising political and military tensions when King Ajātasattu was fortifying the city out of suspicion toward a rival ruler [SuttaCentral; Radich 2011]. In the sutta, the venerable Ānanda is questioned by the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna and the Magadhan minister Vassakāra regarding how the monastic community intends to maintain its unity and discipline in the absence of the Teacher [SuttaCentral; Morrison 2004; Freedman 1977]. Ānanda clarifies that the Buddha did not appoint any single monk as his successor, nor does any individual disciple possess all the qualities of the Buddha [SuttaCentral; Morrison 2004]. Instead, the Saṅgha takes the Dhamma and Vinaya laid down by the Buddha as its refuge and teacher, resolving disciplinary matters collectively by consensus [SuttaCentral; Morrison 2004; Guang Xing 2005; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. Ānanda further outlines ten inspiring qualities (*pāsādanīya-dhammā*) of monks worthy of veneration—including virtue, learning, contentment, attainment of the four *jhāna*s, and the six higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) culminating in arahantship [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. In addition, the discourse discusses two kinds of meditation, criticizing states where the mind remains obstructed by the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and praising the meditation of the four *jhāna*s [Anālayo 2014; Polak 2011].
Curated parallels for MN 108 include *Madhyama-āgama* discourse MĀ 145, the *Saṅgīti Sutta* (DN 33), and SN 22.58 [SuttaCentral]. While MĀ 145 accidentally omits restlessness-and-worry from the five hindrances due to a textual transmission error, MN 108 preserves all five [Anālayo 2014]. Computational text-reuse analysis confirms substantial Pali-internal sharing with the *Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta* (MN 77), the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* (DN 2), DN 33, and various sections of the *Aṅguttara* and *Saṃyutta Nikāyas* [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language alignments by DharmaNexus also match MN 108 with Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* texts (ZH_T01_0026_036, agreeing with MĀ 145), the Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu*, and Tibetan canonical texts including the *Abhidharmakośaṭīkopayikā* (D4094) [DharmaNexus].
